Masters
 DISCLAIMER: The following document is for informational and educational purposes only and does not constitute professional medical, physiotherapeutic, or formal strength and conditioning advice. The physical conditioning, load management, and injury mitigation protocols (such as concussion management and ACL prevention) detailed herein carry inherent risks. Implementation of these strategies should always be adapted in consultation with qualified sports medical professionals, licensed physiotherapists, and accredited high-performance coaching staff. Executive Summary This end-to-end AFL Training Syllabus and Drill Manual serves as a definitive blueprint for coaching across all developmental stages. - Bottom-Line Coaching Philosophies: The syllabus transitions from a play-based, high-engagement model for juniors to a strictly periodized, tactically-driven environment for seniors. The focus shifts from individual ball acquisition and enjoyment to collective spatial domination and match execution. - Physical Conditioning Frameworks: Junior conditioning is disguised as active play to maximize enjoyment and fundamental movement skills (FMS). Youth female pathways mandate stringent, targeted injury-mitigation (Prep-to-Play PRO) to counteract severe anatomical risks. Youth male pathways utilize repeated sprint ability (RSA) to build the anaerobic capacity required for multi-effort contests. Senior football revolves almost entirely around load management, utilizing mathematical modeling (the Banister model) to balance fitness against fatigue. - Top-Level Structural Differences: Junior programs emphasize an 80% focus on technical skill, which aggressively drops to 20% in senior ranks as complex tactical awareness climbs to 60% and physical conditioning load management grows in prominence. Veteran pathways prioritize safety, tissue preservation, and social engagement over high-impact collision and cardiovascular exhaustion. text: 1. Mixed Juniors: The Foundation Phase (Under 8 to Under 14) The junior mixed pathway is the bedrock of football development. The primary objective is fostering a love for the game while systematically building Fundamental Movement Skills (FMS) and technical proficiency in a safe environment [cite: 11, 12]. Under 8 Cohort 1. Developmental Framework & Best Practices Coaching Under 8s (U8) is fundamentally about organized chaos. The coaching philosophy relies on play-based learning and the "SPIR" method (Show, Practise, Instruct, Reward) to teach basic handling and hand-eye coordination [cite: 13, 14]. - Focus Areas: The training ratio demands 80% Technical Skill Acquisition, 10% Tactical Awareness (basic spatial recognition), and 10% Physical Conditioning (disguised as active play). - Communication & Language: Coaches must utilize the "Change It" methodology (varying Communication, Area, Numbers, Game rules, Equipment, Inclusion, and Time) to maintain engagement [cite: 15, 16]. Language must be highly visual and positive, avoiding complex jargon. Structuring these sessions effectively ensures young players remain continuously active rather than waiting in lines, which rapidly degrades their attention and enjoyment. 2. Standard Session Breakdown (90-Minute Blueprint) While standard Auskick sessions traditionally run shorter, a 90-minute advanced blueprint is structured to maximize touches without fatigue [cite: 17]. - Warm-up / Activation (20 Mins): Evasion and tag games (e.g., Calf Tag) to build FMS like hopping, skipping, and spatial awareness [cite: 18]. - Skill Acquisition (30 Mins): Isolated basic handling (rolling, bouncing, ground ball gathers). Focus on individual ball time. - Game Sense (30 Mins): Modified grid games with no tackling, emphasizing "Footy for Kicks" and keeping the ball moving [cite: 12]. - Conditioning & Recovery (10 Mins): Fun relay races that incidentally build aerobic capacity, followed by a calm group debrief. This blueprint ensures physical conditioning is completely integrated into fun activities, masking the fitness element behind gamification. 3. High-Detail Drill Inventory (Drill 1)

the players, the coach freezes the play and asks questions categorized into four concepts: Time (When should you dispose?), Space (Where should you move?), Risk (Which option was safest versus most rewarding?), and Execution (How should you deliver the ball?) [cite: 15].
By guiding players to analyze these four pillars, coaches fast-track the cognitive processing required for executing skills under high-intensity match pressure.
Grounding Game Sense in Reality: The Auskick to U12 Transition Case Study This methodology is not merely theoretical; it is grounded in extensive empirical observation within elite pathways.
For example, a three-year action research study by Deakin University evaluating the AFL Junior Match Policy—which oversees the critical transition of players from Auskick programs into Under 12 junior football—demonstrated the concrete advantages of SSGs over full-scale environments.
Analyzing over 60 matches, the research found that reduced 12-a-side formats on modified spatial dimensions provided vastly more technical actions, touches, and scoring opportunities per player compared to traditional 18-a-side models [cite: 16, 17].
By shrinking the numbers and space, the literature confirms players are forced to execute higher volumes of decisions and possessions under pressure, actively hardwiring their spatial awareness and transition play more effectively than in congested, full-field settings [cite: 17].

WELCOME
Welcome to the Junior Coaching ranks.
The AFL Junior Coaching Curriculum
and its subsequent resources have been
designed for coaches of players aged
7–12 years.
The prescribed training sessions make
it simple and easy for parent and
volunteer junior coaches to deliver.
The program has been developed with
the support of industry experts across
coaching and education and has been
incorporated into the Rookie Me – RM
Coach platform, an activities and
training sessions library, available to
all coaches through their CoachAFL
Membership.
Why do we need a Junior
Coaching Curriculum?
The Junior Coaching Curriculum has
been developed to increase player
transition and retention from NAB AFL
Auskick to Junior football. The key
objectives are to:
A Improve the quality of coaching at
Junior levels and thus subsequent
experiences of the kids that play
junior footy,
B Build on the NAB AFL Auskick
philosophy of high energy and
high touch sessions using small
sided games,
C Provide national consistency in the
standard and delivery of training
content for Junior footy and
D Ensure every training session is
Safe, Organised, Engaging and Fun.
The Junior Coaching
Philosophy
The overarching reason kids play
football is to have fun. There is a
significant connection between the
level of skills a child has and the
amount of enjoyment they experience.
The minute kids stop being engaged,
is when we are likely to lose them.
Ultimately, kids want to get better
at the game so they can get the ball
more and experience some success.

So, just like NAB AFL Auskick,
the Junior Coaching Curriculum is
about the growth, development and
confidence of the kids that train
and play but most of all its about
having fun!

Three Levels of Progression
Building on the success of the NAB
AFL Auskick program, the Junior
Coaching Curriculum is based on three
sequential levels, designed to extend
skill development over three (or more)
years of participation.
LEVEL 4
Designed for players turning 7 and 8 who
are transitioning over from Auskick to
Junior Footy. This level focuses on skills
needed to work as an individual.
LEVEL 5
Designed for players turning 9 and 10
beginning the transition to working in
small groups.
LEVEL 6
Designed for players who are under 11
and 12, focusing on skills needed to work
as part of a team.
Each level consists of a set of 10 training
session plans each with a session theme,
learning outcomes, activity instructions
and diagrams with key coaching points.
For training programs that run for longer
than ten weeks, the base program can be
supplemented with additional sessions,
either by repeating selected sessions or
tailoring to meet the needs of the players.

The Junior Coaching Curriculum has
been designed around the principles of

of the game and follows the premise of
‘using the game to teach the game’.

LEVEL 4 | 7-8 YEARS
4 | NATIONAL JUNIOR COACHING CURRICULUM
A Game-Sense Approach
to Coaching?
A key focus of each training session
is to teach the fundamental skills
of football using game sense and
constraints-based learning approaches.
Skills that are learned within a gamebased context better transfer to the
game, and players develop a greater
understanding of how to play the game.
It also increases energy, motivation and
engagement so that kids have more fun
and want to come back for more!
What is it?
u Playing games to practice skills,
rather than only practicing skills in
isolation of the game (the traditional
approach).
u Games are carefully designed
to emphasise specific skills and
strategies.
u The coach’s role is to question and
guide players towards a better
understanding of the game and the
required skills.
Why use it?
u Children learn to adapt their
technique to game situations;
u It teaches tactical understanding of
the game;
u It appropriately applies the principle
of training specificity.
Transfer of learning from training to
game day depends on the extent to
which training resembles game day.
What is Skill?
The fundamentals of technique are important! But equally important is the
ability to adapt technique to any game situation, and football is a dynamic
game with constantly changing situations. Skill is the ability to execute in
competitive situations that differentiates players and teams.
SKILL = TECHNIQUE + ADAPTABILITY UNDER PRESSURE

What does this mean?
How to explain this
concept to children
ATTACK
Penetration Advancing the ball towards the goals “Get the ball moving forward”
Possession Keeping control of the ball by either
holding it up or making simple lateral
passes until better options are available
“Play keeping’s off until you see a
chance to move the ball forward”.
Support Provide support and safe passing
options to the player with the ball
“Help the player with the ball find
space or create a passing option by
finding space yourself and calling for
the ball”
Movement Moving to create space for both yourself
and others
“Continuous movement to find space
and get the ball”
DEFENCE
Delay Positioning of the defender closest to the
player with the ball to slow the attack by
preventing the ball being moved forward
“Make it hard for the player with the
ball to pass or move quickly”
Pressure Quickly closing down the player with the
ball to minimize the time and space in
which the ball can be controlled, with the
aim of causing a poor decision
“Get close to the player with the ball to
pressure and cause a turnover”

The junior training session structure is designed to sequentially build kids football
skills and confidence over ten training sessions using a game-based approach whilst
incorporating fundamental skill development throughout the program. Each training
session runs for 70 minutes and is designed around the four quarters of a game with a
pre-game activity section for unstructured play.

game and skill development. Refer to the following diagram which outlines the purpose

NATIONAL YOUTH COACHING CURRICULUM 1
SECTION 1
RATIONALE
The Junior Coaching Curriculum (JCC) was developed to increase player transition and retention
from NAB AFL Auskick to Junior Football by providing coaches with a resource of prescribed training
sessions that are age and developmentally appropriate for players aged 7-12 years.
The Youth Coaching Curriculum (YCC) is an extension of the Junior Coaching Curriculum (JCC). It
offers essential guiding principles to assist coaches in nurturing the growth of players and teams
within the 13-18 age range, where a wide spectrum of developmental maturity exists among the
players.

12 children, 5 parents
All children have a ball. Starting in a scattered formation,
children roll the ball (dribble) close to their body and in
control. Five eliminators (parents) are selected. They
attempt to tap the balls away from the children. Using rolling
skills, peripheral vision and body positioning, children protect
their ball. Eliminators must not continuously target the same
child. Once a ball has been tapped away or child goes out
of the playing area, he/she must sit on ball for 10 seconds
before restarting.

right before changing direction. Start with children walking;

Landings are an important safety issue in sports and teaching children how to fall will help prevent injuries.
The aim is to absorb the forces sequentially to cushion the landing.
Landing on feet: Contact with balls of feet, then heels; flex knees, then hips. Finish with feet
shoulder-width apart, body in motorbike position. When leaping (moving forward), land on whole foot.
Landing on hands: Make contact with fingers and palms, flex elbows and shoulders to absorb the force
Falling: When rolling, keep chin tucked in to the chest and allow the body to roll freely.

text:
For volunteer coaches, this can appear overwhelming. Many community coaches receive little formal education before taking responsibility for an entire team.
This reference library has been written to bridge that gap.
Rather than simply presenting drills, it explains why each activity exists, what it teaches, how to coach it effectively and when it should be used throughout a player's development.
Whether coaching Under 8 football or Senior Men's football, the principles contained within this library remain the same:
Create an enjoyable environment.
Maximise learning.
Challenge players appropriately.
Encourage decision making.
Build lifelong participation in Australian Football.
Winning football matches is an outcome of good coaching—not the sole purpose of coaching.
[Heading 1] Chapter 1 – The Role of the Coach
[Heading 2] Learning Objectives
After completing this chapter, coaches should understand:
Their responsibilities beyond winning games.
The different roles they perform during a season.
How coaching responsibilities change across age groups.
The behaviours that create positive learning environments.
The importance of player-first coaching.
[Heading 1] 1.1 What Is Coaching?
Many people believe coaching simply involves selecting drills, choosing a team and instructing players during matches.
Effective coaching is far broader.
A coach is simultaneously:
Teacher
Leader
Organiser
Motivator
Role model
Communicator
Mentor
Planner
Problem solver
Learner

The most successful coaches continually refine their sessions rather than repeating the same program indefinitely.
[Heading 1] 1.5 Coaching Priorities by Age Group
[Table]
Age Group	Primary Coaching Priority
Under 8	Enjoyment, participation and basic movement skills
Under 10	Fundamental football skills and confidence
Under 12	Decision making and teamwork
Under 14	Skill execution under pressure
Under 16	Tactical understanding and consistency
Under 18	Match performance and role execution
Senior Women	Team systems, decision making and physical preparation
Senior Men	Performance, accountability and continual improvement
Masters	Enjoyment, safety, skill maintenance and social connection
[Heading 1] 1.6 The AFCRL Coaching Principles
Every drill, session and season plan within this library is built upon the following principles.
[Heading 3] Principle 1 – Players Learn by Playing
Football should resemble football.
Drills should include realistic movement, decision making and communication whenever possible.
[Heading 3] Principle 2 – Maximise Ball Contacts
More footballs.
Smaller groups.
Less waiting.
Greater repetition.
[Heading 3] Principle 3 – Progress Before Pressure
Players should first understand a movement before performing it under increasing pressure.
A typical progression is:
Learn the movement.
Repeat the movement.
Perform while moving.
Perform under passive pressure.
Perform under active pressure.
Perform in game-like situations.
[Heading 3] Principle 4 – Reward Good Decisions

[Heading 1] Australian Football Coaching Reference Library (AFCRL)
[Heading 1] Volume 1 – Foundations of Coaching Australian Football
[Heading 1] Chapter 3 – Player Development by Age
[Heading 1] Learning Objectives
After completing this chapter, coaches should be able to:
Understand the developmental characteristics of each age group.
Design training appropriate to the physical, cognitive and emotional abilities of their players.
Set realistic expectations for skill development.
Deliver coaching that maximises enjoyment and long-term participation.
Adapt communication styles for different ages.
Recognise when players are ready to progress to more advanced football concepts.
Avoid common coaching mistakes for each stage of development.
[Heading 1] Introduction
One of the greatest mistakes a coach can make is coaching every age group the same way.
An Under 8 player is not simply a smaller Under 18 player.
Children, adolescents and adults differ significantly in their physical development, attention span, emotional maturity, ability to process information and reasons for participating in football.
A training session that motivates an Under 18 squad may overwhelm an Under 10 team. Likewise, activities designed for young children may quickly disengage senior players.
Effective coaches understand where their players are in their development and adapt their coaching accordingly.
The aim of each stage is to prepare players for the next stage—not to rush them through it.

[Heading 1] 9.6 Recovery
Recovery is where improvement occurs.
Training creates stress.
Recovery allows the body and mind to adapt.
Without adequate recovery, players accumulate fatigue rather than fitness.
Encourage players to prioritise:
Quality sleep.
Hydration.
Nutritious meals.
Gentle movement after matches.
Recovery between training sessions.
Recovery should be viewed as an essential part of training rather than an optional extra.
[Heading 1] 9.7 Age-Specific Training Loads
Training loads should always reflect the age and development of the players.
[Heading 2] Under 8–Under 10
The emphasis should remain on:
Enjoyment.
Skill development.
Movement.
Participation.
Avoid prolonged conditioning activities without the football.
[Heading 2] Under 12–Under 14
Gradually increase training intensity while maintaining a strong focus on skill development.
Players experiencing rapid growth may fatigue more quickly and require additional recovery.
[Heading 2] Under 16–Under 18
Training intensity can increase significantly.
Coaches should remain aware of school commitments, representative football and periods of rapid physical development.
[Heading 2] Senior Football
Adult players often balance football with employment and family responsibilities.
Training should be demanding but efficient.

[Heading 2] Setup

Players work in pairs facing each other.
Place two cones approximately 1 metre apart halfway between each pair to create a kicking gate.
Player spacing should be:
Under 8–10: 8–10 metres apart.
Under 12–14: 10–15 metres apart.
Under 16 and above: 15–20 metres apart.
Ensure enough space exists between pairs to avoid footballs crossing into neighbouring groups.
[Heading 2] How the Drill Works
Player A begins with the football.
Player A performs a stationary drop punt towards Player B.
The football must pass cleanly through the cone gate before reaching Player B.
Player B marks or gathers the football.
Player B resets before returning the kick through the same gate.
Continue for the allocated time.
Coaches may award one point for every kick that travels cleanly through the gate without touching a cone.
The emphasis should remain on correct kicking technique rather than scoring points.
[Heading 2] Coaching Points
Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Teach players to:
Maintain the same technique used in KK-001.
Keep the hips and shoulders aligned with the target.
Guide the football directly onto the kicking foot.
Strike through the centre of the football.
Finish with the kicking foot pointing towards the target.
Stay balanced after the kick.
Remind players that a smooth, technically correct kick is more important than a powerful kick.
[Heading 2] Coaching Cues
"Kick through the gate."
"Straight line."
"Head over the football."
"Finish to your target."
"Accuracy before power."

Ball drop consistency.

Player A kicks to Player B.

Player B marks or gathers the football.

Coaches may introduce a simple scoring system:
2 points for a chest mark.
1 point if the receiver gathers the football cleanly after one bounce.

[Heading 2] Coaching Points
Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Teach players to:
Look at the target before beginning the kicking action.
Kick to where the receiver can comfortably mark the football.
Match the force of the kick to the required distance.
Maintain the same drop punt technique regardless of distance.
Stay balanced throughout the kicking action.
Finish towards the intended target.
Players should understand that kicking accurately is more important than kicking hard.

[Heading 2] Setup
Create a directional field.
Mark a central five-metre hot-spot scoring zone at each end.
Mark one wider scoring zone on either side of each hot spot.
Divide players into two teams.
A marked kick received inside the hot spot earns three points.
A receive in either wider zone earns one point.
[Heading 2] How the Drill Works
Teams attack their nominated scoring end.
The possession team attempts to create and use any scoring zone.
A clean mark inside the central hot spot earns three points.
A legal receive inside a wider zone earns one point.
Defenders must protect the hot spot while pressuring the football and wider leads.
A defensive intercept inside the hot spot earns one defensive point.
Following a turnover, the intercepting team immediately attacks the opposite end.
Players may kick or handball outside the scoring zones.
The coach records both attacking and defensive points.
Play continues for three-minute rounds.

The game replicates team defence inside defensive 50, where players must protect the most dangerous central area without conceding uncontested possession elsewhere.

[Heading 2] Setup
Create a directional playing area with two scoring gates at each end.
Divide players into two teams.
Apply controlled legal tackling appropriate to the age and experience of the group.
The coach records each completed tackle that forces the ball carrier to stop, change direction or dispose.
Possession remains live unless the tackle produces a legal turnover or infringement.
[Heading 2] How the Drill Works
One team begins in possession.
The possession team attempts to move the football through either attacking gate.
Defenders apply controlled tackling pressure.
Each completed tackle adds one to the defensive tackle count.
After three completed tackles in the same possession, the defending team earns one pressure point.
The possession team may continue until it scores or turns the football over.
A disposal completed through a scoring gate earns one point.

The game replicates possession chains where repeated tackling pressure forces players to protect the football, release quickly and maintain support around contact.

[Heading 2] Setup

The possession team scores through a receive inside the attacking scoring zone.

2 – Basic coaching knowledge and one main teaching point
[Heading 2] Session Placement
Technical Skill Block
Main Skill Block
[Heading 2] Setup
Create several contact stations with one tackle bag at each station.
A holder stands behind each bag in a stable position with feet staggered.
The tackler begins 2 metres in front of the bag.
A coach should be positioned where head placement and body alignment can be observed clearly.
Players rotate through tackler, bag holder and recovery roles.
Under 8 players should use soft shields, walking speed and shoulder placement only.
[Heading 2] How the Drill Works
The tackler begins in a balanced stance facing the tackle bag.
On the coach’s signal, the tackler takes two or three controlled steps towards the bag.
The player lowers their centre of gravity by bending through the knees and hips.
The tackler places the near shoulder into the lower half of the bag while keeping the head safely to one side.
The arms wrap around the bag immediately after shoulder contact.
The player takes two short driving steps while the bag holder provides light resistance.
The tackler stops on the coach’s call, maintains balance and releases.
Players reset before repeating from the opposite shoulder.
Complete three to five repetitions on each side before rotating.
[Heading 2] Coaching Points
Make contact with the shoulder rather than the head or extended arms.
Keep the head upright and positioned safely to the side of the bag.
Contact below the shoulders and above the knees.
Bend through the knees and hips rather than folding at the waist.

A second player acts as a passive opponent occupying one side of the contest.
The passive opponent does not hold, push or jump.
Rotate all roles regularly.
[Heading 2] How the Drill Works
The feeder identifies one of the four positional markers.
The ruck moves laterally around the contest point to reach that marker.
The player uses shuffle steps, pivots or short crossover recovery steps while keeping vision on the football.
The passive opponent occupies space and forces the ruck to choose a safe path.
Once the ruck arrives balanced, the feeder tosses the football.
The ruck performs a standing or low-jump palm towards a nominated target.

Setup
Position one ball carrier at the base of the area.
Place two supporting attackers ahead and one behind.
Position two defenders between the carrier and forward targets.
One supporting attacker begins moving immediately.
The second enters late from a delayed starting cone.
The defenders decide whether to press the carrier, hold the first target or track the late runner.
How the Drill Works
1. The ball carrier receives and scans the first available options.
2. The early support player presents immediately.
3. The late runner enters after a one- to two-second delay.
4. If the early target has clear advantage, the ball carrier releases immediately.

Setup
Use six to twelve attackers against six to twelve defenders.
Create an unfavourable defensive match-up inside forward 50.
Position one potential help defender and one last-line defender nearby.
Begin the attacking possession 50–70 metres from goal.
Vary whether pressure can be applied to the ball carrier.
Defenders are not told in advance whether switching, helping or holding shape will be best.
How the Drill Works
1. The attacking team gains possession outside forward 50.
2. Defenders scan match-ups and identify the primary danger.
3. The direct defender communicates whether help or a switch is needed.

Defensive match-ups change through rotations, injuries, transition and opposition tactics. Teams must recognise when help or switching is required without creating a larger problem elsewhere.
